steps.title: Numbers don't work quite like English
body: صِفْر (zero) through عَشَرَة (ten) — eleven words, same as any language. But once you start counting things with them, Arabic does something English doesn't.

For "one" and "two" you barely need the number at all: a singular noun already means one, and the dual ending already means two. For three and up, the number is followed by the noun in its plural form.
You'll read all eleven numbers first, then three short sentences that show counting in action.

steps.title: Zero to ten, then counting for real
steps.intro: Read each number aloud, then the three sentences after them. Tap 🔊 to hear any line.

steps.title: One, two, or three+?
steps.prompt: How many books, and how do you know?

options.label: Two — the dual ending on كِتَابَانِ says so, no number word needed
Three — the sentence must be using a plural

steps.explanation: The ـَانِ ending is the dual (see the singular/dual/plural rule) — it already means "two", the way the plain singular كِتَابٌ already means "one".

steps.title: Spot the plural
steps.prompt: What form is كُتُبٍ, and why?

options.label: The plural of كِتَاب, because 3-10 are followed by a plural noun
The dual of كِتَاب, because ثَلَاثَة sounds like "two"
A different word for "book" that only appears after numbers

steps.explanation: كُتُبٍ is كِتَاب's own (broken) plural — the same one from the singular/dual/plural rule — now in the genitive because it follows a number 3-10.

steps.title: You can count in Arabic
steps.message: You read all eleven numbers 0-10, and saw why Arabic counting isn't just "number + noun" — the noun's own form already carries "one" or "two", and 3-10 take their own plural. The full agreement rule for 3-10 is worth its own lesson later — this is the shape of it.
